title: A Week In Indianapolis, IN On A $50,000 Salary
text:
A Week In Indianapolis, IN On A $50,000 Salary

Welcome to Money Diaries where we are tackling the ever-present taboo that is money. We’re asking real people how they spend their hard-earned money during a seven-day period — and we’re tracking every last dollar.

This week: A manager working in conservation who makes $50,000 per year and spends some of it on a Vera Bradley ID zip case.

If you’d like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we’re not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.

Editor’s Note: This diary was written in 2026 and is a follow-up diary. You can read the previous diary from 2023 here. And the previous diary from 2024 here.

Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We’d love to hear your thoughts here.

Occupation: Manager
Industry: Conservation
Age: 36
Location: Indianapolis, IN
Salary: $50,000
Joint Income/Financial Setup: Joint income is around $115,000; it depends on my spouse’s hours. My partner and I have one joint checking account; we both contribute to it each month to cover our mortgage, utilities, groceries, and daily family incidentals. We each have our own checking, savings, credit cards, and loans that we are individually handling. I will be tracking my individual spending as well as our joint spending for this Money Diary.
Assets: $79,692.27 (HY Savings: $2265.15, Checking: $300, Retirement: $66,451.62, Equity half: $10,675.50). I know in my past diaries people didn’t like that I halved mortgage and equity since that wouldn’t really be the case if my partner and I split; but it is how I have calculated my net worth for years, so I’m gonna do me.
Debt: $149,854.18 (Auto lease: $1,995.04, Mortgage half: $143,650.89, Credit cards: $4,208.25)
Paycheck Amount (Every two weeks): $1,500
Pronouns: She/her

Monthly Expenses

Housing Costs: $2,600. I live with my husband, B., and two children, O. (who is six) and A. (who is two). This is paid out of our joint account.
Loan Payments:
Car lease: $500 (I’m planning to buy out my lease before it terms later this year)
Energy/Gas: Average $75; fluctuates with the seasons (paid out of joint). Electricity: Average $185 fluctuates with the seasons (paid out of joint).
Phone/Disney+: $40 (I pay this to my parents for my phone and I cover Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN+ for my whole family; parents, brother, brother/SIL, and my family) (B.’s phone is paid for by his work)
Netflix: $8
Health & Dental Insurance: $500 — deducted from my partner’s paycheck
H.S.A Contributions: ~$140 deducted pre-tax (my partner has auto deductions set up from their paycheck)
Internet: $75 (my partner pays this)

Other Expenses:
Chewy Dog Food: $52 (every five weeks)
Trash: $119 (paid quarterly out of our joint account)
Pest Control: $180 (paid quarterly out of our joint account)
Car Insurance: $1,500 (paid every six months out of our joint account)

Weekly Expenses:
Daycare: $150
After School Care: ~$50 (we pay what we use so this can vary depending on schedules. This week, I ended up paying more because the system is glitching, but that will simply pay us ahead).

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
Yes. Both of my parents are college graduates, both the first in their families (I think my dad’s oldest brother has an associate’s degree but I don’t know if he got that before my dad finished his bachelor’s degree or not), and both have since received their master’s degrees in their respective fields as well. My mother also worked at a college before having us kids and then again once my youngest brother was in elementary school. I attended one college my freshman year in the hopes of receiving a tuition exchange, as my mother worked at another local college. That didn’t pan out so I ended up transferring to the college my mom works at and finishing school there. While my tuition at the school my mother worked at was paid due to her employment, I still took out loans for housing for three years. I lived at home during my senior year to save money.

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
I can’t recall any specific conversations per se, but I remember being taken to the bank at a young age to set up a savings account (we got dinosaurs for making deposits — as a kid, who could ask for a better incentive!). I also remember participating in a club/class that was a mock stock market class while I was homeschooled in elementary school. I remember nothing specific about that class other than that I took it, though. I learned more through watching my parents manage their money from afar.

What was your first job and why did you get it?
I started babysitting at the age of 12 and became a certified babysitter by the time I was 14. My first tax-paying job was at a local T-shirt shop in town when I was a senior in high school. I got that job because I had dropped out of all my extracurricular activities senior year and my parents said I had to do something. I loved the job and ended up working there several summers into college.

Did you worry about money growing up?
I didn’t. If there were family struggles, I didn’t know about them. I have a general idea of what my dad made when I was younger now, which was somewhere in the mid-$90K range. I know as he climbed through a few companies, he was able to leverage his skills for higher pay. We were comfortably upper-middle class. My mother stayed home with us after my first brother was born and she homeschooled us all once we got to school-age. I was homeschooled until I went to sixth grade and my mom stayed home until my youngest brother was in fourth grade. We were blessed enough to have more than we needed on my dad’s job alone during these times.

Do you worry about money now?
Yes. Very much. I recently left my previous position, in a move that I didn’t want to make but felt forced to. This meant I had to take a significant pay cut, which will probably set me back around three years in salary. I’m in my third week of work at this new location and so far it has been great, but the pay is a big question mark. I should get my first paycheck within this week, so right now I’m not certain what my paycheck will look like. The nice thing is that I’m now salaried and my pay will be stable from pay period to pay period. There is also now the question of my commute, which has tripled despite me working from home two days a week now. Lots of question marks so far!

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
Other than staying on my parents’ insurance until 26, around 23 I moved out on my own and handled all of my own bills. Currently, our safety net is our savings, then our parents. All three sets of parents (my parents, FIL & Step-MIL, and MIL) would help us out if we were in a pinch and have offered many times prior when we needed it.

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
Yes. My parents paid for our wedding. Also, my parents typically gift us money for Christmas each year and we get varying amounts of cash from my husband’s parents for holidays and birthdays.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day One: Tuesday

6:25 a.m. — My final alarm goes off and I get up and head to the shower to start my day. We had a rough night last night because we had storms and some tornadoes go through our area; the kids slept fine but one of our dogs has extreme storm anxiety so she was a wreck most of the night and kept us up. After my shower, I get the kiddos, A. and O., up and they snuggle in my bed with B. for a little while I get dressed in a floral button down and jeans.

7:10 a.m. — We’re on our way to school and sitter drop-off. Most mornings I take our Kindergartener to school and B. takes our two-year-old to the sitter. We get to school right when the doors open, so that’s a quick process.

7:45 a.m. — I make a quick detour on my commute to a traveling coffee truck which is set up perfectly along my route this morning. Normally, I don’t get to stop except on Thursdays when they’re scheduled to be set up at a hospital on my route; on Tuesdays they don’t have a set location so this was a blissful happenstance. I get a cold brew with a small splash of cream; something that should be easy but this coffee truck is the only place that consistently gets the “small” splash correctly. It’s simple and delicious. $8

8:30 a.m. — I’m the first one to arrive at the office, which has been typical so far into this job. This is my third week, and while the workday officially begins at 9 with the commute time, it doesn’t make sense for me to go back home after dropping off my kiddo, so I just head in and get there whenever. This office is wonderfully flexible and I have so far enjoyed the people and the work I’m able to do with them. I settle in. I get an email notification that our son’s after-school care weekly payment is due (in the weekly expenses). My coworkers, who are in the office today, start arriving around 9:15 a.m. and we quickly catch up and share our storm stories from the night before.

12:00 p.m. — I take a break to make my lunch. I have tomato soup and dry ramen noodles for texture. I took this job after leaving my previous position after nearly 15 years. While it was not what I wanted to do by any means, I loved the people and the work; circumstances changed and it felt like I didn’t have a choice. I had previously been doing two jobs and it was at a point those jobs needed to be separated; I made it clear to my boss which of the two positions I wanted but I felt that was ignored, and I was offered the opposite. I was informed that was my only option if I was to stay. I believe the offer was made with the hope of me staying out of loyalty. I chose to leave as I didn’t think it was fair after 15 years that my opinions on my own position weren’t considered or shared with the board of directors. It has been a rough year so far.

4:00 p.m. — The workday ends and I head on my way to pick up my kids. We have an evening T-ball game tonight for my oldest, so we are boogying as fast as we can to get going as we have to get home, get O. dressed, get snacks and get to the ballfield ASAP.

7:15 p.m. — T-ball finished, delightful chaos as usual. A. got to play with a new friend of hers at the field and we got to visit with three of the five grandparents. Since it is so close to bedtime, we capitulate and stop at Taco Bell for a quick dinner. $18.30

8:45 p.m. — Everyone is fed and in bed, including B. and me. Hopefully, we have a full night’s sleep. (Reader, as expected, this did not happen).

Daily Total: $26.30

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Two: Wednesday

6:30 a.m. — After a rough night of both dogs and kids being up multiple times, it is time to get up and get everyone motivated. Thankfully, I work from home on Wednesdays, but everyone else has to get to where they are going. Kids are finally up and fed, and we are out of the house and in place just in time. I’m wearing a T-shirt and jeans, and a fluffy sweater because it is pretty chilly here today.

11:00 a.m. — I scheduled a grocery pickup this morning so I’m out of the house and picking that up ($172.41 from our joint spending). Then head back home for lunch and more work. I also do lots of laundry and empty the dishwasher during my day when I have a chance. $172.41

2:00 p.m. — Picked up my son from school for early release; get home and settle in O. with some books so I can get back to work. I also realize that we were missing several items from our grocery order and request those to be refunded. ($23.65 refunded to the joint account).

4:45 p.m. — I pick up A. from the sitter after my workday ended. I realize I have two more items that I didn’t get with my grocery order and request those refunded, too. ($5.41 refunded to our joint account). We get home and the kids play while I lounge around for a bit and do some cleaning. B. gets home later than usual tonight, so dinner is a bit of ‘choose your own adventure’ for us. We play with the dogs and snuggle the chicks. (Oh, I totally forgot to mention that we not only have two dogs but we recently added three chickens to our home. We are raising them for eggs and once they are a little bigger, they will move outside into the coop that B. is building. Currently, they are living in a pen in our garage and we are loving the tiny chicken snuggles and the chaos that they bring.)

9:30 p.m. — Kids are in bed. B. and O. spent the evening building with Lego, so I put A. to bed tonight. I’m snuggled into bed and playing a dumb game on my phone while B. makes himself a very late dinner. I turn on my current rewatch of Star Trek: The Next Generation and settle in for silly space adventures. Love me some Commander William T. Riker. In the hope of a better night’s sleep, I pop my earplugs in and drift off.

Daily Total: $172.41

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Three: Thursday

6:30 a.m. — Up a little later than usual and in the shower. O. got himself up with his Yoto alarm and greets me at my bathroom door, scaring the bajeezus out of me! O. asks if he got up early enough for pink donuts. He has been asking all week, but hasn’t gotten up early enough to go get a treat, so this morning he was a self-starter. I’m dressed in jeans and a fleece sweatshirt. B. and O. head out for breakfast treats. A. and I take a leisurely approach to the morning since I don’t have to be in the office until 9. We enjoy our coffee and “coppee milk” in our vintage diner tea cups and chat about all the interesting things that two-year-olds know. Then we get her dressed, put in her two pigtails, and tell the chickies to have a good day and get in the car.

12:00 p.m. — I have been settled in at my desk for a while now and was the only person in our office until after 10:30. I’m highly considering moving my laptop into our conference room because work is being done on the building right outside of my window, and they’re hammering on the wall. It’s not the easiest way to concentrate on work. One of my coworkers forgot their lunch so they suggest we all hop in the car and head to Sweetgreen. I get a guacamole greens bowl with tofu. $17.49

3:45 p.m. — Head out for my daily commute home. I only have to get A. this afternoon. O. is being picked up by my dad and they’re getting dinner, and going to see a program with a Benjamin Franklin reenactor at our local college as part of the celebration of the 250th anniversary of the US. So it is just A. and I for a while until B. gets home from work. We get lots of snuggles and giggles in.

8:30 p.m. — O. gets home from his evening with grandad. He is disappointed that A. is already in bed, but is happy to play for a while with just me while B. works on finishing our chicken coop. After a while of play and some reading, O. heads to bed and B. and I shortly follow as well.

Daily Total: $17.49

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Four: Friday

6:30 a.m. — Finally a night of pretty good sleep! Kids are in our bed and we snuggle for a few minutes before getting up and getting ready for the day. O. asks to be a ‘lunchboxer’, so I grab a Lunchable from the fridge for him. He doesn’t often ask to bring his lunch, so I try to keep a few of these on-hand for a quick grab since he usually makes the request last minute before we leave for the day. B. takes A. to the sitters and I take O. to school. I’m in a T-shirt and sweatpants to start my day.

8:00 a.m. — I sit down to my laptop at home. Friday is another work-from-home day for me, so I can start early and finish early if I get everything done. I check and I can see that my first paycheck hit my bank. It is more than I anticipated so that is great, while it is still a large-ish pay cut from what I was making prior, but it is not as bad as I worried it would be. I work through my budget adjustments and then realize I have plenty of room to do some ordering for things for A.’s room. We recently moved her into her own room after the kids had shared since she was around eight months old. I am still working through decorating it and making it something she can grow into. I also get some groceries delivered to make up for the things that got left out of my other order. $60.07

10:15 a.m. — Got a call from school that O. is having tummy trouble. Head out to pick him up. He is in a jovial mood when I get him, but since he told the school he was having bathroom issues he has to go home. He says he is glad I came to keep him company. Get home and get settled back in for work and O. watches some Star Wars show on Disney+. O. had requested donuts since he was missing a friend’s birthday party at school today. I had already been planning on getting donuts for the weekend so I go ahead and order those for delivery from our local donut shop. $27.62

3:45 p.m. — Wrap up the work day. Swing by the bank to get the cash for our sitter $150 (in weekly expenses) and head to pick up A. After picking A. up, O. says his belly feels bad and he wants a barf bag for the ride home. Thankfully, he doesn’t need to use it and is feeling better, but tired when we get home. I let O. play a little more of his video game because A. said she wanted to watch, and O. tries to teach her how to play, which is very sweet. O. has recently become obsessed with Star Wars and my brother got him a Lego Star Wars video game for Christmas, which has been a huge hit. While the kids do that, I start working on a travel Lego case idea I found on Pinterest because I am sick of free-floating Legos in the back seat.

5:45 p.m. — B. gets home from work and heads outside to work on the coop for a while, with the help of O. We end up having quesadillas for dinner and B. picks the family movie for the evening. We wind up watching Man Of The House on Disney+. It’s quite the ’90s throwback. We ended up letting the kids stay up way later than usual, but now everyone is snuggled into bed and lights are out. I stay up wayyyyyyy too late just scrolling on my phone.

Daily Total: $87.69

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Five: Saturday

6:15 a.m. — A. is screaming, “Mommy come get me!” from her bedroom. Not upset screaming, just attention screaming. I grab her and hope to settle her into our bed to snuggle and go back to sleep. That doesn’t happen; she instead crawls all over me and asks for snacks and Mickey Mouse Clubhouse+, and on and on and on. She finally gets down and asks her dad to take her to the living room. Saturday is my day to sleep in, so B. takes A. to the living room. I hear O. shortly after I get up and follow them out.

12:15 p.m. — I got two extra hours of sleep and after getting up at 9:00 a.m. I make my coffee and have a slow start to my morning. We gear up and get ready to head to O.’s T-ball game. I get dressed in jeans and a long-sleeved T-shirt, and a sweater again since it is chilly, as well as my team hat. Our T-ball league gives all the teams names after the pros, so each year I buy myself a hat for the team O. is on. Armed with snacks and bubbles for A., we head out. We meet up with nana and grandfather at the ballfield and enjoy a good game. O. was excited to tell us that he was going to try to hit the ball off the pitch both times he bats, and how he will do this. I have been pleased with his effort this season; he is willing to learn and be a good teammate, which has been very fun to watch.

5:00 p.m. — I get a call from my mom about dinner tonight; they are inviting us over to watch the Kentucky Derby. We have already started cooking so I pivot and invite them over since we have plenty. We do a quick clean of our house, mainly to wrangle the toys into the playroom and clean off the whole table since I have been using that as my workspace. They come over for burgers, fried potatoes, and my mom made some mac and cheese. Then we watch a very exciting race and cheer very loudly for the FIRST FEMALE horse trainer to win the derby! Let’s hear it for women in sports!

8:00 p.m. — My parents leave and we are gearing up for bedtime. O. asked earlier in the week if he could put A. to bed and we forgot last night, so we offer him the opportunity to do her bedtime tonight. I get her changed and ready and send them into her room to read a book after bedtime kisses. It lasts about six minutes before I can hear negotiations taking place with A. yelling, “don’t leave, O!” and O. trying to tell her he is done. I go in and the lights are still on, so clearly they weren’t headed for bedtime. I get the lights turned off, the sound machine on, and the night light on and let O. and A. snuggle for a bit and sing to them before O. says he is done. I send him on his merry way and finish up bedtime for A.

9.00 p.m. — O. is headed to bed with B. I start reading a library book, And Now, Back to You by B.K. Borison, on my Kindle that’s due back in a few days. I don’t get very far reading it before I switch to scrolling and B. comes in for bedtime.

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Six: Sunday

6:45 a.m. — Another early wake-up for A. at around 6:45 a.m. B. grabs her and puts her in our bed. O. has joined us, too. A. leaves our bedroom to go play. She is usually pretty good at self-entertaining (this comes back to bite me). We snuggle for a little bit then O. and I get up and let B. sleep in.

8:15 a.m. — We walk into the kitchen and see the egg carton on the floor. A. has taken it off the counter. I check the carton and there are 11; this was a full carton before. I speak to A. about not playing with food and then ask her where the other egg is. She tells me it is in the playroom, but says, “It not broken, mommy.” Thankfully, it was on our indoor/outdoor rug — but it absolutely is broken. A. is sorry, and says she won’t do it again. O. decides he wants to watch some cartoons and I make my coffee and get the kids breakfast. A. finds some chapstick and wants to use her “wips”. This again ends in disaster as she uses it on the floor, on a Polly Pocket, and on a picture of her cousins.

3:00 p.m. — We have an exceedingly lazy day today. The kids play and I read most of my book. B. plays games on his phone. A. is up early from her nap and snuggles, and watches Mickey Mouse Clubhouse with me while I read. I order a Target delivery since we need diapers to take to the sitter’s tomorrow for A. $45.84

7:30 p.m. — Kids are both in bed and snoring. We had a little bit of a rough evening: the kids both threw fits when they were asked to clean up the playroom. But everyone rounded the corner for dinnertime and we had early bedtimes all around.

8:30 p.m. — I climb into bed and finish my book. Very cute, enjoyed the sweet relationship featured, and while not super steamy, there was just enough for a quick read. B. is in bed and we are both scrolling on our phones; I am looking through grocery lists and planning for our week. Neither of us is too sleepy, so B. turns on a movie. I promptly fall asleep after that. (Also as note, I did not change out of my PJs today — pure lazy bliss!)

Daily Total: $45.84

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Seven: Monday

6:20 a.m. — I am up and in the shower. O. got himself up again this morning and is sitting in his room when I go to check on him. A. is a slow wake this morning but then is out and about and coloring with O. in the living room while we get ready. I get dressed in green linen pants and a navy and white polka dot button down for work since I am in the office today. I flip the coffeemaker on, and I’m so thankful that I prepped it last night before bed. We are just about ready and out the door when I realize O. hasn’t taken his inhaler today and he has already been coughing up a storm. I run back in and search to no avail. I tell him on the way to school to go see the nurse, as she has one of his inhalers on hand. After dropping him off I top up on gas and head to work. $50.01

8:30 a.m. — At the office and get right to work building my brand new office chair. Very excited to not be sitting at a glorified kitchen chair. Everyone else slowly rolls in. I also put in an order for batteries, a teacher appreciation gift, and a new Vera Bradley ID case. I had forgotten how much I loved those in college and something like that still makes sense for me as a daily carry. $36.36

11:15 a.m. — We have our standing department meeting and one of our leadership team informs us that she has turned in her notice and will be leaving the staff in early June. I am sorry to hear this, but also understand since I too recently left a job I loved. She and I had actually had a preexisting relationship. I will definitely miss working with her.

1:45 p.m. — I see a reminder that my son’s elementary school choir group is singing the national anthem at a minor league baseball game this Friday, so I text B. about getting tickets to go. He is all for it so I hop online through the fundraising link and get us three lawn tickets; thankfully, A. is still free. $49.74

4:30 p.m. — Kids and I are home now. They want to play ‘car’, which means they sit in the front seat of the turned-off car and pretend to drive. O. cleaned out the backseat so I could sit there. He lasts all of three minutes before he realizes his friend is also outside and he runs across the street to their house with promises that he is just going to say hi. He ends up staying over there for a while, so A. and I finish playing ‘car’ then head into the garage to visit the chickens. O. brings his friend back over to ours to play for a bit before dinner. They run all over the front yard, help themselves to popsicles and have a grand old time before his friend gets called home for dinner.

5:45 p.m. — B. arrives home and we all head in to start making our dinner. I also get to hanging the curtains I got for A.’s room. Chicken patties and fries for dinner. We enjoy chatting about everyone’s day. I also place a grocery order to pick up later this week (we will be charged at pickup). A. is in bed around 8, but unhappy about it and crying. I am not pleased with the new curtains; they aren’t as room-darkening as I had hoped. After I leave A.’s room, I do a return to Target for those. I will get $24.40 refunded. I look through Amazon for another option and find something in a similar color that promises full blackout; I add new sketchbook for O. and some water bottle straws. $48.50

9:15 p.m. — I take a bath and start reading another book by an author I will be seeing in person at an event later this week. I can hear A. still crying; B. goes in to calm her down. During that process, O. opens his sister’s door and tries to ask his dad something and wakes A. I get out of the bath, B. leaves A.’s room, she is still screaming, and O. starts to get ready for bed. We have a talk with O. about not going into his sister’s room after bedtime since he woke her up. B. puts O. to bed and we let A. cry for a while until she falls asleep. I hate doing that, but she was clearly overtired and won’t stay asleep if we stay in her room with her. B. comes to the bedroom and showers. Our younger dog is also in our room, which doesn’t bode well since we expect storms overnight. We are finally all tucked in and I turn on a sleep story on Calm. Fingers crossed the night isn’t too rough.

Daily Total: $184.61

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Breakdown

Conclusion:
This is my third time writing a Money Diary. I always enjoy doing the narrative portion as I do track all of my expenses on an app already. This was a pretty typical week, for the most part. Most of my spending is on groceries and gas, so that all made sense. I have also gotten better about actually returning things that don’t work for us and making sure I am getting refunded for groceries that aren’t either of good quality or aren’t actually part of our order. With money being tighter for us, not just because of my job change, but also because of the current economic state, I’m more anxious around our money than normal but trying to make easy changes that make sense for our family.

title: What We’re Not Talking About When We Talk About Ariana Grande
text:
What We’re Not Talking About When We Talk About Ariana Grande

Content Warning: This article includes discussion of eating disorders.

Ariana Grande is currently the internet’s main character — but it’s for a pretty distressing reason. Over the past several years the Petal singer and Academy Award-nominated star of Wicked has been everywhere. But recently, the conversation around Grande hasn’t been about her performances or her latest album, but rather her body and increasing concerns over her health as well as speculation that the singer may be grappling with an eating disorder.

This isn’t anything new. In 2024, conversations around Grande’s body began to swirl during press for the Wicked franchise, after Grande and co-star Cynthia Erivo were photographed looking noticeably thinner; causing people to speculate on the reasons for the pairs’ weight loss. In 2025’s Wicked:For Good, Grande looked even more frail. More recently, videos of Grande performing onstage during her Eternal Sunshine world tour looking malnourished elicited further comments of concern from fans online, culminating in a furor on July 31 when Grande released the music video for “Petal,” the title song off her latest album of the same name.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Ariana Grande (@arianagrande)

In the video, Grande plays a very clear version of herself; an auditioning actress named Pepper who’s repeatedly told she’s not good enough and needs to change, tweaking herself with every audition to fit the clearly unattainable expectations of the industry. Grande appears throughout the video looking thin and frail, most noticeably in one scene where she dons a black bodysuit reminiscent of Sandy in Grease. Since its release, the comments of the video have been flooded with concern from fans, writing: “It’s not about wanting the old Ariana back. It’s about wanting her to be healthy.” Another fan commented: “Seeing her ribcage and clavicle is truly terrifying. I hope she gets the help she needs soon or at least someone close to her steps up.”

Shortly after the video was released, Grande’s team issued a statement revealing that the pop star will be stepping back from the spotlight after her current tour and dropping out of co-starring in the previously announced stage production of Sunday in the Park with George alongside Jonathan Bailey. In a statement to People, a representative for Grande said: “Ariana will be taking a step back from visibility after she completes the Eternal Sunshine Tour. She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny,” the rep continued. “This tour has been a beautiful experience for her. She loves her fans and has loved every minute of this tour so much.”

Needless to say, it’s complicated — and people online are divided. The past several weeks have seen fans, trolls, and fellow celebs alike take to the internet to share their thoughts on Grande’s health and body, with comments ranging from genuine concern to insensitive statements that she should “just eat a cheeseburger” and debates over whether or not we should be talking about Grande’s body at all. 

On August 1, model Tess Holliday took to Instagram to share her opinion on the conversation, asking people to retire “the public body commentary era.” 

Around the same time, The Good Place actress Jameela Jamil took to social media to share her concerns for the star, replying to a post about the latest video, writing: “This poor woman is possibly dying right in front of us,” before criticizing her team as “irresponsible” for making decisions that clearly emphasize her small frame. Jamil was quickly criticized for her comments, before doubling down; emphasizing that it’s a complicated situation, but emphasizing that not saying anything means “we run the risk of normalizing that image to hundreds of millions of teenage girls, kids and even impressionable adults consuming her content.”

Actress & advocate Jameela Jamil made a comment of concern on Ariana Grande’s appearance in her recently released ‘Petal’ music video. Do you think the discourse is valid?

(📸: YOUTUBE/INSTAGRAM) pic.twitter.com/Fd6CLix9oz

— OK! Magazine USA (@OKMagazine) August 2, 2026

So, how should we be talking about Ariana Grande? It’s not so clear cut. With the help of experts and people dealing with the complexity of eating disorders personally, we sift through the discourse and its dangers.

Should talking about Grande’s body be off limits? The answer requires nuance.

For dietitian, author and the writer behind the Rethinking Wellness newsletter, Christy Harrison, this conversation swirling around Grande isn’t necessarily all that new. As any person, especially women, knows, celebrity bodies, especially celebrity female bodies, have always been heavily scrutinized.

And while often unfair, it makes sense that these people would be topics of conversation, given the role modern celebrities and their images play. “They’re held up as symbols of beauty,” Harrison tells Refinery29. “These images are not just a person’s own.” Instead, these celebrity images are carefully  manufactured by record labels, PR teams and other facets of the celebrity image-making machine to be viewed as idealized beauty standards or a goal that fans should strive to and want to emulate – at least to the point of purchasing what they’re selling; be it concert tickets, beauty lines or lifestyle. 

“There’s always this dynamic, there is always this conversation between what celebrity culture and Celebrities Inc. is pushing out there and then how the public is receiving that and responding,” Harrison says. Essentially, these images are being put out to be consumed, so it’s natural that consumers would have thoughts about them. “If this is what’s swirling around in the culture, if this is what’s publicly being put out there as someone’s image, I think the public has a right to a discourse about it,” Harrison adds. 

For Harrison, what is different about the current conversation around Grande from those of celebrities in the past, is the polarization in reactions online; a reality Harrison says is partly due to social media algorithms, which prioritize hot takes for virality instead of nuance. 

Another key difference for Harrison? “Ariana Grande is very emaciated.” 

While Harrison emphasizes that we don’t know the specificity of Grande’s health, as she’s not shared anything publicly, “bodies that dramatically thin — we’re not talking about standard celebrities – we’re talking about this level of thinness that is concerning I think to many people; it raises alarm bells because of its association with sickness, stress, it makes it seem like there’s something going on…I think that’s part of what has created this sort of heightened moment about the discourse around her body. People are understandably feeling concerned for her, and there’s alarm bells going off that something isn’t right.”

We don’t need to know Grande’s medical history to know she’s clearly going through something — and we need to discuss that with care

While Dr. Courtney Simpson, Director of the Eating Disorders Centre at the Evidence Based Treatment Center of Seattle, agrees with Harrison about not speculating on an individual’s health, she points to Grande’s long career and visibility in the spotlight. Since she first came onto our screens in 2010, the public have seen Grande — and her body — through various stages as she’s gone through puberty and young adulthood. That is no doubt a difficult position for Grande; something she has spoken about openly, often exploring the parasocial relationship between herself and her fans in her music. In 2024’s “Yes, And?” Grande addressed this head on, singing: “My face is sitting, I don’t need no disguise / Don’t comment on my body, do not reply / Your business is yours, and mine is mine.” 

But for Simpson, this time in the spotlight also serves as an indicator that something is at least different with Grande and her body right now. “With someone like Ariana Grande, we have seen her body change over time,” Simpson says. “And so there’s evidence to support that something’s going on there; whether it’s an eating disorder or not — you can have other conditions that can contribute to losing a bunch of weight.”

While Simpson notes that you can’t necessarily tell that someone is struggling with an eating disorder by just looking at them, “she doesn’t look healthy or well,” Simpson says.  Which means, for Simpson, that conversations around Grande’s body, weight and mental health need to be handled with care “Whatever the cause, [we should be] thinking about framing the conversation as: something appears to be going on that’s contributing to her looking malnourished and that’s concerning,” Simpson says.

And, Grande shouldn’t be attacked and vilified for this. Much of the initial conversations around Grande and her weight painted it as a moral failing of sorts. This goes back to the parasocial relationship many fans have with celebs. In a 2011 interview with VOGUE, Rihanna infamously said she didn’t want to be a role model, and time and time again we’ve seen instances of celebrities held to higher standards by their fans and the public due to their visibility. But what’s lost in this inherent expectation is the fact that, at the end of the day, Grande is a human being, meaning she’s not always going to — and maybe can’t necessarily — make the decisions the public deems as “correct.”

“Eating disorders specifically…they’re not a choice,” Simpson adds. “They’re not something that someone chooses, they’re not something that somebody one day wakes up and [says]: this is fun. It’s a complex interaction between biology and environment.”

But at the same time, Ariana Grande is a public figure, and that can come with consequences

While Grande and her team may just want public scrutiny to go away, the thing is that, it can’t. Celebs like Grande may not have signed up to be role models for the masses, but the truth is that by virtue of their roles and their success, they inevitably have become that. Meaning that what they do, say, and yes, even how they look, sends a very public message about what’s accepted and viewed as the norm — and that can negatively impact young people or trigger those who are currently grappling with or in recovery from an eating disorder.

A 2024 global study from the University of Waterloo found that 55% of youths surveyed between the ages of 10-17 felt dissatisfied with their bodies, with social media as a large factor impacting this. And the conversation around Grande’s body, as well as “concern trolling” comments online have reportedly caused an influx of calls to eating disorder helplines in the UK, with clinicians reporting clients who are upset about the constant scrutiny and public comments about Grande’s body. 

As journalist Nicole Russel noted in an opinion piece for USA Today about Grande, “it’s a double edged sword: Her celebrity status doesn’t exempt her from scrutiny, but that scrutiny should stay constructive and kind.” Especially when, as Russell points out, her health and appearance are topics of conversation based on a music video she herself would have produced and approved. 

Madison Mazzeo has experienced the impact of this firsthand. The 31-year-old Phoenix-based podcaster is currently in recovery for an eating disorder, something she has dealt with since she was 16-years-old. As someone who was initially in a larger body, she says, “the thing that’s actually been the most triggering to me is watching people applaud [Grande’s] body and applaud its changes and defend it.”

“I got a lot of comments about being in a larger body and so the second I got into a smaller body, people were all telling me how much healthier I looked and how good I looked. I feel like she [has] had a pretty similar trajectory,” she says of Grande.  

Both Harrison and Simpson have also encountered clients feeling activated or impacted by both the conversation around Grande’s body as well as the overall return to extreme thinness in society right now with the proliferation and increased accessibility of weight loss drugs.  

“The thing that happens with our brains is that the more that we see a certain type of image, piece of information, the more we get used to it and the more it becomes normalized,” Simpson says. “What that means is that we’re getting used to that as a standard, even if we’re not trying.” 

And constantly reinforcing the message that this is what a healthy body does — and should — look like. 

For both Simpson and Harrison, this concern is especially pertinent for young people, whose media literacy skills and ability to discern and think critically about the images in front of them are still developing.”It’s not just concern for her, it’s concern for ourselves and the fear that the beauty standard is shrinking to ever-smaller proportions in a way that I think we fear that’s going to become what’s expected of us as women,” Harrison adds. “As everyday women, that’s the new standard that we’re going to have to adhere to, not just unattainably thin, the way that we’ve seen from celebrities for decades, but distressingly thin perhaps thin to the point of illness or something going on that just feels like this could actually be deadly.” 

And it’s this concern — and impact — that takes this particular conversation beyond the typical refrain to never talk about women’s bodies — because this is an extreme example. As journalist Stacy Lee Kong noted in a recent edition of pop culture newsletter Friday Things, the idea that it’s taboo to talk about celebrities’ weight and bodies makes sense philosophically, especially when you look at examples like the fatphobia inherent in comments about singer Adele’s thinner body in 2020. But as she says, it doesn’t entirely make sense to expect people to ignore when a celeb’s appearance changes, considering that’s the currency they tend to run on. And it’s especially nonsensical to use the idea of never talking about women’s bodies as an excuse to not address potential real-world harm. 

Are these conversations helping people with eating disorders? We need to think about the message this debate sends.

With all that being said, it’s important to also take a larger look at the people and systems surrounding Grande right now, and question them, too. 

The announcement from Grande’s team noted that the pop star would be taking a step back from the spotlight, because of the “endless, ongoing public scrutiny” it has led to; reinforcing that Grande is healthy. For Mazzeo, this framing, for a celebrity with such a large platform, is not only problematic, but also potentially harmful.  “There’s a difference when you’re in the public eye and you’re like, ‘Hey, I’m struggling with an eating disorder’ versus I’’m the healthiest I’ve ever been and you shouldn’t assume otherwise,’” she says. While Mazzeo notes that Grande doesn’t owe us transparency on whether or not she’s dealing with an eating disorder (or another illness), it’s the constant assurance that she’s fine and healthy that’s an issue. “Because I think that is very dangerous, to be clearly malnourished and tell everybody that you’re healthy,” she says. 

And there are many people behind the scenes that would go into that decision. As Stacy Lee Kong says in the same Friday Things newsletter, it’s important to ask questions about what’s really happening here. As Lee Kong asked: “Why is her team so invested in portraying her as healthy and happy? Do they really have her best interests at heart, or are they invested in protecting her tour’s profitability? What professional responsibilities are at play here?”

“Celebrities are a business,” Harrison says. “A business in line of fire is always going to say ‘everything’s great’ or ‘we’re listening and learning’ or ‘we’re taking some time to reflect.’ This is a common trope. It’s not specific to her situation, it’s damage control.”

What remains important is how we, as the public, engage in conversations around Grande’s appearance with those in our lives. For people viewing these images who may feel impacted by them, Harrison suggests taking a social media break and stepping away from the discourse if you’re able to. “Getting back into real life, getting some support, getting some help for your own disordered eating or body image distress, that’s really what’s most important.”

If you are struggling with an eating disorder and are in need of support, please call the National Eating Disorders Association Helpline at 1-800-931-2237. For a 24-hour crisis line, text “NEDA” to 741741.

title: You’re Invited To Meet NYFW’s Next Generation Of Designers
text:
You’re Invited To Meet NYFW’s Next Generation Of Designers

When you look at the traditional New York Fashion Week calendar, the barriers to entry aren’t a secret. Between massive production budgets, rigid legacy structures, and steep venue costs, incredible independent talent is too often priced out of fashion’s biggest stage. That’s why this season, Refinery29 is officially teaming up with RAISEFashion to shift the narrative.

On September 11, we’re co-hosting The Penthouse Edit at The Standard, East Village. It’s a full-day, high-impact showcase designed to put fashion’s most exciting emerging designers directly in front of the industry’s top buyers, editors, stylists, and power players.

What’s even better? It’s open to the public, and you’re invited too. To secure your spot on the guest list, RSVP directly at the following link.

This isn’t just another presentation; it’s a dedicated platform for sustainable growth and real equity in fashion. We’re spotlighting the need-to-know names spanning ready-to-wear, luxury accessories, and fine jewelry. Each one is proof that the industry’s next era is being built on craft, community, and fresh perspectives.

Moving the needle in fashion requires capital, space, and access. We’re taking over the venue’s crown-jewel top floor alongside a group of partners who understand the importance of supporting independent talent.

Afterpay is stepping up in a major way for fashion’s next generation, co-hosting the event and dropping dedicated funding initiatives to fuel growth this season. Crown Royal is keeping the drinks flowing and awarding its own production grant during our VIP September 10th kickoff cocktail hour. (Bonus: You can shop the limited-edition Crown Royal x Juicy Couture capsule right on site, with proceeds going straight into the grant fund.) To top it off, we’re hosting an on-site shop featuring talent from Victoria’s Secret’s Runway to Revenue accelerator, giving you a chance to shop fashion’s next wave before everyone else.

Each of the names below is proof that the industry’s next era is being built on community. Get to know the designers shaping the next generation below, and stay tuned as we bring you exclusive insider coverage straight from The Penthouse Edit.

Almasika

Founded by Catherine Sarr, ALMASIKA transforms global heritage into a distinct language of fine jewelry. Drawing from years in the luxury diamond sector—including pivotal time at De Beers—Sarr leverages sculptural forms and noble materials to create symbolic, heirloom-quality pieces rooted in universal human connection.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Campillo

Designed by Patricio Campillo, Campillo reimagines traditional Mexican tailoring through a modern, artisanal lens. DashDividers_1_500x100

K.ngsley

Founded by Kingsley Gbadegesin, K.NGSLEY is an activist-driven fashion brand known for its distinctive cut-out tanks, subverted basics, and body-conscious silhouettes. Rooted in Black, Queer, and Trans liberation, the label blends high-fashion construction with nightlife culture to create powerful, gender-inclusive ready-to-wear.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Le Blanc Studios

Co-founded by Angelo and Yamil Le Blanc, Le Blanc Studios is a Dominican-rooted streetwear and ready-to-wear label that channels Caribbean heritage into refined urban apparel. Blending military-inspired utility, historical narratives, and structural tailoring, the brand offers a sophisticated commentary on identity and movement.

Fine jewelry designer McKenzie Liautaud creates balance-minded, artisanal pieces that harmonize global travel with geometric elegance. title: ghd’s New Interactive Hair Styler Is So Impressive, I Ditched All My Old Hot Tools
text:
ghd’s New Interactive Hair Styler Is So Impressive, I Ditched All My Old Hot Tools

Like most of my journalist peers, I view AI with a healthy dose of antipathy. Call me a Luddite, but I don’t want my jewelry to tell me I’m not getting enough sleep or a bottle to scold me when I forget to drink water (it’s pretty often).

There are times, though, when I’ll gladly accept help from the machines, and one of them is taking the chore out of styling my hair. Happily, ghd seems to think it has cracked the code with its brand-new Sculpt Interactive Straightener.

ghd Sculpt Interactive Hair Straightener, $449

What is ghd Sculpt and what are the benefits?

Sculpt is ghd’s first-ever “interactive” styler. According to the brand, it’s “powered by AI that senses, learns and adapts to your hair’s temperature” — monitoring it 2,900 times per second, no less — “for personalized styling.” So, what exactly does that mean? Five times faster styling compared to the ghd Original straightener, better curl definition compared to the ghd Chronos straightener, and 2.5 times less frizz (but more on those later).

Perhaps the most impressive benefit, though, is no heat damage. Impossible, I hear you say! But it makes complete sense. The plates are packed with sensors that measure how much hair is between the plates, how quickly you’re going, and the angle at which you’re holding the tool. All of these factors send information to the sensors, which then decide how much heat you need and, more impressively, how much heat you don’t need. So instead of turning your straightener all the way up to a scorching 230° and keeping it there, the tool itself decides what your hair needs, minimizing damage such as split ends and color fade over time.

Of course, I’d always recommend using some form of heat protection. For me, that comes in the form of styling products, and I like Kérastase Elixir Ultime Hydrating Hair Oil, which not only moisturizes parched strands but also protects against heat and friction from styling.

What makes the ghd Sculpt Interactive Straightener special?

It was top London hairstylist Samantha Cusick who really convinced me, though. At the preview, I watched her conjure up a head full of waves on a model with thick hair worthy of a shampoo commercial in just five minutes flat — and it’s all down to the artfully designed plates.

“Infinity” plates, to be exact. Unlike the OG ghd straighteners, which have a sharp, clunky edge, these boast what the brand calls “waterfall” edges, so there are no seams per se, just a smooth surface all the way around. If you ask me, this makes the tool so ergonomic that, when it comes to creating waves, each section of hair appears to twirl itself into the plates, going in dead straight and coming out as a perfectly formed, almost accidentally perfect tousle — no snagging whatsoever.

Then there’s the shine. ghd promises 90% more versus naturally dried hair, and I can vouch for that. Each wave emerges from the plates with the kind of gloss usually only achieved using tools with dangerously high temperatures — what I thought I needed, since my hair is both thick and naturally curly.

What to know about ghd’s Sculpt Interactive Straightener:

• Personalizes temperature based on hair thickness, movement and styling angle, delivering more or less heat where needed for zero heat damage.

• Features slim “infinity” plates with smooth, waterfall edges, making light work of both straightening hair and creating waves.

• Promises 90% more shine, 2.5 times less frizz, and styles up to five times faster than the original ghd straightener.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How do you use ghd’s Sculpt Interactive Hair Straightener — and is it worth it?

It’s one thing watching an expert use a tool. The real proof was using it at home myself. While I consider myself something of a beauty expert, hairstyling always evades me, mainly because I’m impatient. Going slow with a straightener? I’m more of a ten-speedy-passes kind of person. Curling irons are a mystery to me, too, especially the ones with a clamp. With Sculpt, I can get pin-straight hair and two different types of wave — depending on which angle I hold the straightener — in moments, and it never feels like a chore.

To create a simple barrel-esque wave, I simply feed a section of hair into the plates from the mid-lengths, clamp down and twist the tool away from my face with both hands, pulling the hair through. Even better, I can save time by taking much larger sections of hair. Because these straighteners are so high-tech, the wave they create is just as perfect as when I feed through half the amount of hair with my ghd Chronos — the tool before Sculpt. When brushed, my hair looks professionally blown-out. I also love fashioning cool-girl S-waves by alternating the direction of the twist as I work down the section, creating a soft, undone bend. As for straightening, the plates feel slender and much easier to maneuver than my trusty ghd Chronos, making it easier to reach the roots and flatten frizz. Thanks to the temperature sensors, it takes fewer passes to make my curly hair straight, too.

Final thoughts

I was convinced that nothing could replace my ghd Chronos, but the Sculpt is smarter, niftier, and faster — and, for the first time, I actually don’t dread styling my hair in the morning. I’m also convinced that my hair is in better condition, too. It feels softer, springier and healthier, which could be thanks to the clever temperature control.

Where can you get ghd’s Sculpt Interactive Hair Straightener?

ghd’s Sculpt Interactive Hair Straightener retails for $499 and is available at ghd.com.

Nuance Nails Are The Creative Upgrade To The Clean Girl Manicure

If our favorite manicurists’ Instagram feeds are anything to go by, the “clean girl” manicure is officially on its way out. Taking its place? “Nuance nails”.

If, like us, you’ve been enamored with sheer pinks and barely-there nails (think OPI Bubble Bath and Essie Ballet Slippers), this is your sign to mix it up a little. Dreamed up by Japanese and Korean nail artists alike, this manicure trend is multifaceted. Think mismatched details, realistic marbling, color gradients, and nail art that mimics all manner of precious stones, from amethyst to emeralds.

What is the nuance nail trend?

Nail artist Emily Brady at Melting Mango Salon tells Refinery29 that this type of manicure looks best on a layered, translucent base — but anything goes. The beauty of the “nuance nail” manicure is that it doesn’t need to be perfect, and each nail can be totally different depending on your mood.

Instead of being tidy and identical, this manicure is certainly more cool-girl approved, hints Brady. “Nuance nails are a step up from the clean girl aesthetic,” she says. “They can still stay super neutral [if you want], but have something that adds a little sparkle to a ‘soap nail’ manicure.” She adds that there are quite a few layers, textures, and blending involved. For those who are still attached to the “clean nail” life, Brady thinks this is a more intricate alternative. “It allows [you] to elevate [your] everyday manicure without being too loud,” she explains.

title: The Future Of Young Hollywood Is Bright, Thanks To These Rising Stars
text:
The Future Of Young Hollywood Is Bright, Thanks To These Rising Stars

It’s a common misconception in Hollywood that instantaneous breakthroughs happen overnight. Academy Award winner Michael B. Jordan summed it up best a month before taking home the Oscar in March, telling Vanity Fair that the weirdest thing about Hollywood is that it “doesn’t glorify the hard work.” In other words, what looks like an overnight success is almost always the result of patience, preparation, and staying the course. The come-up deserves to be recognized. And Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood event last week did just that by celebrating the entertainment industry’s next generation of rising stars.

Held at the Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles at Beverly Hills, the star-studded event honored Tyriq Withers with the New Leading Man Award; Tate McRae received the Triple Threat Award; Sombr was presented with the Songwriter of the Year Award; and Malachi Barton was recognized with the Rising Star Award.​

Year after year, Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood event remains an industry highlight, not only for gathering the best of promising young talent in one room but also for creating an exhilarating atmosphere that affirms creatives that their work has an impact. In an industry that’s quick to move on to the next new and promising face, Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood creates a space (even if it’s just for one swanky evening) for emerging actors, musicians, reality stars, and digital creators to pause and truly relish in their accomplishments. It’s a rare occasion for this business to celebrate the moment they’re in, but the sense of reflection was palpable throughout the night.

​While accepting his award, Withers shared that navigating the entertainment industry has come with its challenges, often taking shape in doubt and feelings of inadequacy.​

“For a long time, I didn’t feel like I deserved to be in places like this,” he said. “As an artist, I grew up believing that there would be some sort of endpoint. I get to the top of a mountain, but only to realize there’s many more mountains left after that.”​

The actor continued, “I thought I would wake up one day and feel like I had arrived. I believed I would stop doubting myself and finally be worthy of the opportunities that were in front of me. But it’s funny because it doesn’t really work like that. I think we all can agree on this. The truth is, I’ll never be ready. The only way to is through, and the best thing I can do is show up as the best version of me.”

​For the actor, receiving the New Leading Man Award has a double meaning. In the literal sense, Withers has graced the big screen starring in Reminders of Him (2026), Him (2025), and I Know What You Did Last Summer (2025). In July, Deadline announced that the Atlanta actor will star opposite Isabel May for the upcoming romantic comedy, Love Love. And while it’s every actor’s dream to play the lead across projects, Withers also sees that honor as a call to action for the type of person he wants to be not just in his professional life, but personal too.​

“If I want my career to stand for anything, I hope that it’s leading with love,” he continued. “This award says New Leading Man. I don’t get that as a title. I get that as a challenge –an invite, if you will. An invite to keep chasing and choosing stories that ask those different questions. An invite to keep collaborating with people who make me better. An invite, most importantly, to keep staying curious.”​

McRae, who recently headlined her first Lollapalooza drenched in liquid gold, was honored for being a triple threat poised for popstardom.​ Known for her high-production stage spectacles, the singer, dancer, and songwriter admitted that her over-the-top persona is her superpower.​

“I have a slight problem with doing the most at all times,” she said. “But honestly, I think that obsession has always been the thing that drives me. When I love something, I really love it. I want to know everything about it. I want to get better at it. I pretty much let it consume my entire life.”

​Singer-songwriter Sombr was recognized for dominating global airwaves and charts with his breakthrough smash hits such as “Back to Friends,” “Undressed,” and “12 to 12.” Before turning 21 in July, he hit major milestones that typically take many artists decades to reach.  ​

“I write all my songs alone in my bedroom, and to be recognized in this incredible setting is humbling,” he said. “Songwriting is the reason I’m alive. My mind can go to dark places, and it feels like the only thing I can turn to is writing songs.”​

He continued, “While songwriting is technically my job, it’s really my therapy and outlet. It’s my way of speaking when I don’t have the ability to do so any other way.​

From his debut album “I Barely Know Her” making the top 10 on the Billboard 100 to being Grammy-nominated for Best New Artist, the musician used his acceptance speech to thank his fans for making his career possible. He said, “I’d like to thank my fans because I would not be on this stage without them. I love my fans.”

​Malachi Barton rose to fame as a child actor, finding early success in shows like Stuck in the Middle, Instant Mom, and Henry Danger, among others. He’s set to star in the upcoming Disney threequel, Camp Rock 3. Despite growing up in the acting world, Barton knows greatness takes time and that it’s a journey that’ll be worth the wait.​

“I love that this award says Rising Star because you’re not done rising,” he said. “You’re still climbing. You’re still learning, taking risks, and getting better. That’s exactly how I feel.”

​Hosted by Mario Lopez and his son Dominic Luciano, the event also featured a live musical performance of “Pure” by British singer-songwriter Sienna Spiro.

title: The Total Solar Eclipse in Leo Is Here — & It’ll Change Your Life For Better Or Worse
text:
The Total Solar Eclipse in Leo Is Here — & It’ll Change Your Life For Better Or Worse

The first eclipse of the summer is here! The Total Solar Eclipse in Leo occurs on August 12th at 1:36 p.m Eastern Time, causing emotions to soar and the hands of fate to work overtime. If you’re lying beachside in northern Spain or cruising in Iceland, be sure to take cover because this intense lunation is changing our lives for better or worse.

Eclipses bring matters to light, as the moon moves between the sun and the Earth. They offer us a unique look at dynamics and situations, offering us the opportunity to grow. The focus of The Total Solar Eclipse in Leo is to look at our lives from a different perspective, recognizing that outdated belief systems or relationships need to evolve. Leo is a fixed sign, so moving toward a new path of consciousness is going to be challenging. The road we’ve been walking on is splitting into two different paths; it’s up to us to choose the one that connects with our own spirit. Before jumping into something shiny and exciting, take the time to make decisions by first weighing up the options. Eclipses make us feel like it’s now or never, and it’s not. Tempering our energy with rationality and pragmatism is the best way to proceed. 

The caveat is that we might not want to make changes; however, if we don’t do the work, then we will stay stagnant, or the universe will take the upper hand and transcend our lives for us, without our control. As you may have experienced in the past, the eclipses can be a little nasty if we’re not open to taking strides and a leap towards transformation. This eclipse in particular is close to the South Node of Destiny in Leo, so it’s forcing us to release what is no longer working in our lives.  

Fernando Salinas, tarot reader and author of The Joy of Tarot, explains: “Leo does not like being upstaged, and as it is ruled by the sun, a Total Solar Eclipse in Leo feels particularly tense. What does a show person do when the spotlight dims? How does a leader lead when they become invisible to their followers? This solar eclipse is occurring at a point in the sky that signifies a release of these expectations to be showy, and will help us all realize how we can shine without being seen and how sharing the limelight makes us all a little brighter. The Strength tarot card, which is associated with Leo, reminds us that compassion and grace are also ways of being strong, and this solar eclipse is going to help us put this into practice.” 

This eclipse comes into contact with Saturn retrograde in Aries. So, expect frustrations with authority, or those who are bossy, since we are resisting their domination and commands. Firmly leaning into our own power and being noncompliant with their projections encourages us to firm our own thoughts and beliefs, allowing us to evoke the positive nature of Leo. Simultaneously, we have to contemplate and activate the North Node of Destiny in Aquarius; this gives us a sense of altruism. We aren’t sitting idly by watching everything happen; we are taking action to defy the status quo and invigorate our lives.

Black Moon Lilith, as well as the asteroid Lilith, both of whom are in Sagittarius, and the asteroid Pallas in Aries, are firing up the energy. We want to be free and will do anything to fight for our independence. If that means cutting off people who are holding us back from being the truest versions of ourselves, then so be it. This isn’t an eclipse where we are hiding from reality; rather, we are confronting circumstances because we wish to shine and sparkle in our radiance. It’s about time people shower us with respect. It starts with the way we treat ourselves — the solar eclipse is a reminder of our fabulousness. 

There will be a moment of vexation because an ego death is happening; however, it doesn’t necessarily allude to an ongoing struggle in our lives, as long as we are releasing people and things that are not part of our journey. The destination may bring us back together with them, but it’s okay to part ways temporarily and to focus on ourselves.

title: Mars In Cancer Is Here — & You’ll Be Taken Out Of Your Comfort Zone
text:
Mars In Cancer Is Here — & You’ll Be Taken Out Of Your Comfort Zone

Watch out — this summer, the planets are still being messy. Mars’ dance in Cancer from August 11th to September 27th highlights honesty, nostalgia, and passive aggressiveness. We’re being taken out of our comfort zones as we stand up for what we believe in. 

Mars is considered to be in its “fall” when in Cancer, which means that the planet of aggression and action tends to behave indirectly rather than being confrontational. Mars in Cancer will find different ways to assert itself, veering from the norm. For example, this energy pushes us to flirt with our ex’s bestie instead of sending a text to get their attention. Also, Mars in Cancer alters its flow every few days, as the sign and phases of the moon (the planetary ruler of Cancer) are always evolving; it’s hard for us to be consistent.

Don’t be disheartened as there are some amazing attributes of Mars in Cancer. On a good day, Mars in Cancer genuinely cares for loved ones, offering protection and nurturing. This placement will go to extremes to help those it adores. History speaks louder than words, so Mars in Cancer defends those who share memories and are like family. The loyalty Mars in Cancer displays is like no other — especially when the chips are down for a friend or family member. Not forgetting that Mars in Cancer’s intuition is strong, prevailing in moments of uncertainty and confusion. All the more reason why it leads with its gut. 

This year, Mars’s cancer is going to bring an interesting mix our way. The transit starts with Mars aspecting the centaur Chiron on August 12th, which is retrograde in Taurus. At that moment, we are looking inward and how we can use our hearts to heal. On occasion, we may feel as though others have let us down, resulting in anger and defensiveness. There’s an opportunity to recover from the drama as long as we are gentle with ourselves and less critical, trusting in the process of mending situations. Keep in mind that this is a journey that is nonlinear and takes time. 

Then Neptune retrograde in Aries squares Mars in Cancer on August 17th, making us feel as though we are stuck in a moment. The caveat is that we are trying to make waves immediately, but the stars are causing stagnation. To deal with this energy, it’s best to stop in our tracks and to take the day off from willfully taking charge of matters. Instead of trying to fit a square peg through a circular hole, focus on self-care. Our dreams will happen tomorrow or sometime in the future, just maybe not on August 17th, so don’t take it personally if we’re told “no,” because this is just a chance for us to make changes and pour more passion into our visions. 

The most intense day of Mars’s dive in Cancer occurs on September 1st, when it aspects Saturn retrograde in Aries. Questions and issues with authority figures arise, such as who is the boss, because we want to be the one who makes the rules and rebels against the status quo. Being demanding isn’t going to help the situation, even though we think it will. The exact opposite is true — sometimes you have to play the game and slay them with kindness. The reason is that strategy is vital, giving us the motivation to steer the wheel in the way we please by having control over circumstances.

Mars in Cancer’s celestial swim finalizes with a fraught aspect to Chiron retrograde in Aries on September 27th. Again, there is the potential to work through issues; however, taking another look at the past may be triggering. Centering our focus on the relationship we have with ourselves could lead to accountability. Doing so is complicated because it means that we have to be aware of how we’ve hurt others and the role that we’ve had in situations. September 27th brings us face-to-face with our oppa, encouraging us to have the conversations to get the scoop on how to move forward and evolve. Yes, Mars in Cancer is going to be emotional and intense, but at the end of the transit, we may feel more compassion and empathy for ourselves and better understand how we can make improvements in our lives.

This is one of the most astrologically active weeks of August, with the main event arriving on the 12th: the New Moon Total Solar Eclipse in Leo, the first Leo eclipse in over a decade. Solar eclipses accelerate new beginnings, and with this one taking place in bold, passionate, main-character Leo, you may already feel life pushing you toward a version of yourself that’s more confident, creative, visible, and willing to take risks. Opportunities can appear quickly, relationships can shift, and desires you’ve been sitting on may suddenly feel impossible to ignore. You don’t need to have a massive manifestation ritual planned either. Sometimes the eclipse is the intention, and what unfolds around you shows you exactly where this next six-month chapter wants to go.

The fiery energy is amplified by Mercury entering Leo on the 9th, making our communication more expressive, courageous, playful, and occasionally dramatic. We’re more willing to say what we mean, pitch the idea, flirt first, share the post, or admit that yes, we actually do want to be seen and celebrated. Then Mars enters Cancer on the 11th for six weeks, bringing sensitivity and domesticity into this otherwise fiery season. Our intuition gets stronger, home and family matters require more attention, and we may feel fiercely protective of the people and spaces that make us feel safe. Watch for moodiness, passive-aggressiveness, or acting from old emotional triggers when saying what you actually feel would save everyone a lot of time.

Ultimately, this is a week of rapid transformation that feels perfectly aligned with the Fire Horse energy of 2026. The Leo eclipse wants movement, courage, and enough self-trust to follow an opening even when you can’t predict exactly where it leads. Pay attention to what accelerates around the 12th rather than trying to control every detail of your fresh start. The next six months can radically transform the area of your life activated by this eclipse, and your job right now is to stay open enough to recognize when the universe has already started moving the pieces.

Say what you need, listen to what the other person needs, and use this transit to create partnerships where both people actually feel considered.
